title: Why does 7 come up so often?
hook: Two dice can make any total from 2 to 12. So every total is equally likely?

knows: a fair die shows 1 to 6 equally often
probability as a share of equally likely cases
doesNotKnow: that totals of two dice are not equally likely
counting the ways an outcome can be made

misconception: Each total from 2 to 12 is equally likely, since each is a possible result.
objective: The learner can explain that each of the 36 (first, second) pairs is equally likely, and a total's chance is the number of pairs that make it: 6 ways for 7, 2 for 3, so 7 is three times as likely.

claims.text: Two fair dice give 36 equally likely (first die, second die) pairs.
claims.source: 6 x 6 ordered outcomes of two independent fair dice; PAIRS in src/demos/probability/why-seven-wins/model.ts.

claims.text: A total of 7 can be made 6 ways (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) and a total of 3 only 2 ways (1+2, 2+1), so 7 is 3 times as likely as 3.
claims.source: Enumeration (ways() in model.ts): totals 2-12 have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 ways.

claims.text: The middle total, 7, can be made in the most ways.
claims.source: Same enumeration: 6 ways is the maximum.

claims.text: The stage's 1,000 rolls gave 171 sevens and 53 threes.
claims.source: rolls() in model.ts, seed 36, untuned (the first seed tried); ratio 3.2. Over seeds 1-500 the 7-to-3 ratio in 1,000 rolls had middle 95% 2.27-4.23 (median 2.97): a run of 1,000 wobbles, which the reveal says.

recall.question: With two fair dice, which is more likely: a total of 6 or a total of 11?
recall.why: Count the pairs: 6 can be made 5 ways (1+5, 2+4, 3+3, 4+2, 5+1), 11 only 2 ways (5+6, 6+5). 5 to 2 is 2.5 times.
